Extricate

EK-strih-kayt -- from Latin extricare ('to disentangle'), from ex- ('out of') + tricae ('hindrances, perplexities'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To extricate to get someone or something out of a trap, tangle, or difficult situation that holds it.

Volunteers spent the better part of the afternoon working to extricate the stranded kayaker from the fallen tree blocking the river.

Worked Example

Realizing too late that the contract locked her into five more years of payments, she spent months with a lawyer trying to extricate herself from the agreement.

That effort to work your way free of something that has you tangled up or stuck -- whether physically or legally -- is exactly what it means to extricate yourself.

How Extricate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

disentangle

disentangle: to free something from a tangled or complicated situation

release

release: to set something or someone free

Antonyms

entangle

entangle: to cause something to become twisted together or trapped

ensnare

ensnare: to trap someone in a difficult situation

How Strong Is It? — disentangle → extricate → release

disentangle vs. extricate

disentangle vs. extricate: Disentangle is milder than extricate: you disentangle a kite string from tree branches, while to extricate trapped miners is a graver, more forceful rescue from a situation that truly holds them.

release vs. extricate

release vs. extricate: Release goes further than extricate: to extricate the miners is to work them painstakingly out of the wreckage, while their release is the more absolute endpoint — completely and finally free.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ex-

prefix — ex-: out of (Latin)

root — tric-

root — tric-: hindrances, perplexities (Latin (tricae))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ex- ('out of') plus tricae ('hindrances, tangles') plus the verb suffix -ate. To extricate something is to work it out of a tangle of obstacles.
